title: Many Needles in a Haystack: Active Hit Discovery for Perturbation Experiments
claim: Many high-value targets lie in separate modes, so a closed loop of choosing, testing and updating can find them all.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; 3D scatter then cyclic loop with zoomed inset
description: The left panel is a 3D UMAP scatter of gene embeddings. Points are colored from blue (low response) to red (high response). A translucent gray plane marks the 'Top 10% threshold'. Three starred genes (ITGAV, CYB5B, EYA4) sit in separate red peaks, which shows that the high-response region has several modes. A gray funnel connects this panel to the right panel. The right panel shows a 1D curve with several peaks. Dashed teal curves labeled T-2 and T-1 are earlier surrogate estimates, and a solid navy curve is the current one. A dotted threshold line τ and orange stars mark the hits. A loop of arrows runs from 'Choose Candidates' to 'Run Experiments' and back through a green 'Update' arrow. Small bacteria, microscope and petri dish icons illustrate the lab step. The eye goes first to the colorful scatter, then follows the arrows around the loop.
caption: (a) 2D UMAP gene embeddings of Achilles features with the Z-axis denoting phenotypic response to sensitivity of leukemia cells to cytotoxic activity in human NK cells and colors indicating threshold levels. ITGAV, CYB5B and EYA4 are representative genes from three separate modes. (b) Overview of our closed-loop experimental design system. In each cycle, the algorithm samples a batch of genes from a probabilistic surrogate model. These are sent to the lab for validation through real-world (in-vivo or in-vitro) experiments. Finally, the surrogate is updated through the empirically generated responses.
abstract: High-throughput gene perturbation experiments can test several genetic interventions in parallel, yet experimental budgets remain limited. A central goal is hit discovery: identifying as many perturbations as possible whose phenotypic effect exceeds a predefined threshold. Pure exploration strategies are statistically inefficient, wasting budget on low-value regions. Bayesian optimization methods offer a principled alternative but target a single global optimum, over-exploiting dominant modes while neglecting other high-value regions. We formalize hit discovery as a sequential experimental design problem and propose Probability-of-Hit, an acquisition function that directly targets threshold exceedance by ranking candidates according to their posterior probability of being a hit. We prove asymptotic optimality of this approach and demonstrate strong empirical performance on both synthetic benchmarks and real biological immunology datasets, including up to 6.4% improvement over baselines on the Schmidt IL-2 dataset.
